_comment: The English prose of the historical database. It mirrors the French file entry for entry: every source, every figure label and every observation is translated, and the loader still lays this file over the French one field by field, so anything left blank here would read in French rather than not at all. The identifiers are NOT translated — they are rebuilt from historical-figures.json, which holds the numbers, the dates and the addresses and is never duplicated per language.

minfin-fnb-2021-10.title: Information release on the results of the investment of the resources of the National Wealth Fund — position at 1 October 2021
minfin-fnb-2021-10.organisation: Ministry of Finance of the Russian Federation
minfin-fnb-2021-10.note: Monthly release of the Russian Ministry of Finance, the fund's own issuer. The file name carries the reporting date, so the address cannot be silently replaced by a later month. The document gives TWO distinct amounts: the total volume of the fund and, separately, the “obyom likvidnykh aktivov” — the volume of liquid assets, defined by the Ministry itself as only those sums deposited in the fund's accounts at the Bank of Russia. The rest is locked up in deposits at VEB.RF, in bonds and in shares of Russian issuers. The file was downloaded from this address and its text extracted; reading the HTML pages of minfin.gov.ru directly, by contrast, requires a workaround tool. This source says nothing about the central bank's foreign exchange reserves, which are an entirely separate item.

minfin-fnb-2022-01.organisation: Ministry of Finance of the Russian Federation

minfin-fnb-2022-03.title: Information release on the results of the investment of the resources of the National Wealth Fund — position at 1 March 2022
minfin-fnb-2022-03.organisation: Ministry of Finance of the Russian Federation
minfin-fnb-2022-03.note: First reporting date published after the invasion and after the freeze of 28 February. The document is decisive for understanding the trap of this item: its “liquid assets” line still counts 38,561.6 million euros, 4,178.7 million pounds sterling and 600,304.0 million yen — currencies that Western sanctions had just made unusable. At that date the Ministry's “liquid” line therefore measures what the fund OWNS, not what Moscow can SPEND, and the source does not draw that distinction.

conseil-ue-immobilise-g7-2024-02-12.title: Immobilised Russian assets: Council decides to set aside extraordinary revenues — press release of 12 February 2024
conseil-ue-immobilise-g7-2024-02-12.statedUpdate: Press release dated 12 February 2024 at 17:14; carries “Last review: 28 January 2025”
conseil-ue-immobilise-g7-2024-02-12.note: This is the source that fills the gap identified. The Council writes there in so many words: “Around €260 billion in Central Bank of Russia assets have been immobilised in the form of securities and cash in the jurisdictions of the G7 partners, the EU and Australia, with more than two thirds of those immobilised in the EU.” The perimeter is exactly the one sought, and it therefore encompasses the €210bn for the EU alone already present in the database. The address carries the publication date in its path. Where it stops proving anything: it is a rounded order of magnitude fixed in February 2024, never refreshed by the Council since, and it is a valuation of a stock of securities and cash, not an audited inventory jurisdiction by jurisdiction. The country-by-country breakdown does not appear there, and Australia is not quantified separately.

eprs-confiscation-2025-09.title: Confiscation of immobilised Russian sovereign assets: State of play, arguments and scenarios — briefing PE 775.908
eprs-confiscation-2025-09.statedUpdate: Document dated September 2025 by its publisher; reference PE 775.908
eprs-confiscation-2025-09.note: The file name carries the year and the reference number, an address that cannot be silently replaced. The briefing serves here as a CONTROL on the Council's figure: it recalls the February 2024 amount — €260bn for the EU and the other G7 countries — and adds that, including non-G7 countries, the world total would approach €300bn. Its figure 1 details a total of €289.5bn for 2025: European Union 209.2, of which Belgium 180, Japan 28.1, United Kingdom 26.6, Canada 15.1, Switzerland 6.2, United States 4.3. Note that this perimeter is NOT the Council's — it adds Switzerland and does not isolate Australia — and the EPRS itself states that these amounts come from calculations by PISM and the Swiss federal government, not from an official declaration by the holding jurisdictions, and that the exact value per jurisdiction is hard to establish for want of consistent official information. This figure therefore cannot replace the Council's, only bracket it.

conseil-ue-fnb-interdiction-2025-12-12.title: Council decides to prohibit transfers of immobilised Central Bank of Russia assets back to Russia — press release of 12 December 2025
conseil-ue-fnb-interdiction-2025-12-12.statedUpdate: Press release dated 12 December 2025 at 19:35; carries “Last review: 16 December 2025”
conseil-ue-fnb-interdiction-2025-12-12.note: A source with no figure in it, retained for a single point of law, verified in the text: the regulation of 12 December 2025 prohibits any transfer of assets of the Central Bank of Russia “or of any legal person, entity or body acting on behalf of, or at the direction of, the Central Bank of Russia, such as the Russian National Wealth Fund”. It therefore establishes that the National Wealth Fund is named in the European freeze, and that it must not be treated as an item sitting outside the sanctions. It says nothing about the amount of the fund held in the Union, and the Council publishes none.

kiel-ust-r30-fichier.title: Ukraine Support Tracker — Release 30, full data workbook (“ReadMe” sheet)
kiel-ust-r30-fichier.organisation: Kiel Institute for the World Economy
kiel-ust-r30-fichier.statedUpdate: The ReadMe sheet describes itself as “Ukraine Support Tracker — 30th release (covering January 24, 2022 to June 30, 2026)” and carries the date 30 June 2026
kiel-ust-r30-fichier.note: File downloaded (12,155,823 bytes) and opened here with openpyxl: 95 sheets. This is not a search-engine summary. The file name carries the release number, so the address cannot be silently replaced by a later version. The ReadMe fixes the vocabulary on which everything else depends: “We report ALLOCATIONS as our primary metric. Commitments of future aid are reported in auxiliary figures. When information on deliveries or disbursements is available, we report these as well.” A commitment is an announcement, an allocation an assignment to a concrete package, a disbursement a payment observed — and the tracker publishes the last of these only where the information exists. This file proves what governments have ANNOUNCED and ASSIGNED; it stops proving anything the moment you ask it what reached the front.

kiel-ust-r30-fig-a31.title: Ukraine Support Tracker — Release 30, sheet “Fig A31 Monthly Avg 2022-2026” (Monthly Average of Aid Allocations by Donor Group: 2022–June 2026, billion Euros)
kiel-ust-r30-fig-a31.organisation: Kiel Institute for the World Economy
kiel-ust-r30-fig-a31.note: This is the dataset UNDERNEATH the “Aid allocations by donor group” chart read off by eye until now: same three groups, same two types, same five periods. The values are now read in the cell, no longer off a bar height. Structure of the table: rows 12 to 16 = 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026; columns E, F, G, H = military (United States, Europe, Other donors, Total); columns I, J, K, L = financial and humanitarian (the same four). The formulas sum column Q of the bilateral database — “tot_sub_activity_value_constant_currency” — hence CONSTANT EUROS, adjusted for inflation and exchange rates, 2021 base (the Country_Deflator sheet writes “Currency Power Change (2021 = baseline)”). Explicit filters in the formula: measure = allocation, type = Military or Financial & Humanitarian, month within the bounds of the year. “Europe” = EU member states and institutions, Norway, United Kingdom, Iceland, Switzerland. “Other donors” = Australia, Canada, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea, Türkiye, China, Taiwan, India. The sheet says nothing about what was delivered: allocation only.

kiel-ust-r30-fig-2.title: Ukraine Support Tracker — Release 30, sheet “Fig 2. Country Groups (stacked)” (Aid allocations and residual commitments across donor groups, billion Euros)
kiel-ust-r30-fig-2.organisation: Kiel Institute for the World Economy
kiel-ust-r30-fig-2.statedUpdate: Release 30, cumulative from 24 January 2022 to 30 June 2026
kiel-ust-r30-fig-2.note: The sheet publishes side by side, for geographic Europe and for the United States, the cumulative COMMITTED and ALLOCATED, and the gap between the two. It also gives the definition the tracker uses: “Allocations are defined as aid which has been delivered OR SPECIFIED FOR DELIVERY” — an allocation therefore includes equipment earmarked but not yet on its way. That is precisely why allocation is not delivery. Amounts in CURRENT euros (the formulas go back to columns M and P of the database, undeflated), unlike the Fig A31 sheet. The sheet does not quantify the “Other donors” group.

kiel-ust-r30-aggregates.title: Ukraine Support Tracker — Release 30, sheets “Aggregates by Country Group” and “Fig A22. Cumulative Alloc.”
kiel-ust-r30-aggregates.organisation: Kiel Institute for the World Economy
kiel-ust-r30-aggregates.statedUpdate: Release 30, cumulative from 24 January 2022 to 30 June 2026
kiel-ust-r30-aggregates.note: “Aggregates by Country Group” breaks commitments and allocations down by country and by sub-group (EU, Anglo-Saxon countries, other donor countries, geographic Europe), in billions of current euros, across the three types of aid. “Fig A22” gives the cumulative monthly series and its end point at 30 June 2026. These sheets do not follow the group split of Fig A31: the “Other donors” total in the sense of the chart has to be rebuilt by adding Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the “Other donor countries” block. That addition is done here and flagged as such. Known discrepancy between the two sheets — €179.80bn against €179.34bn of military aid allocated — because the monthly series excludes allocations with no month assigned.

kiel-ust-r30-fig-9.title: Ukraine Support Tracker — Release 30, sheets “Fig 9. Budget Support by Donor” and “Financial disb per Month (€)” (Foreign budgetary support: allocations vs. disbursements)
kiel-ust-r30-fig-9.organisation: Kiel Institute for the World Economy
kiel-ust-r30-fig-9.note: THE source on actual disbursement, and the only one that gives amounts for it. It covers a single category: budgetary support to the Ukrainian state — loans, grants and guarantees paid into the budget. The disbursements do not come from the tracker but from the UKRAINIAN MINISTRY OF FINANCE, that is, from the recipient, which makes them a control independent of the donor. The sheet specifies “nominal value”: CURRENT euros, not adjusted for inflation. It proves nothing about military aid, nothing about humanitarian aid, and nothing about what the weapons that actually arrived are worth.

kiel-ust-r30-inkind.title: Ukraine Support Tracker — Release 30, sheets “In-kind Military per Country”, “Fig A4. Weapon Delivery” and “Delivery Transparency Index”
kiel-ust-r30-inkind.organisation: Kiel Institute for the World Economy
kiel-ust-r30-inkind.note: The second and last window the tracker offers on what was delivered. It is in NUMBERS OF UNITS, never in euros, and it is limited to five categories of heavy weapons: 155/152 mm howitzers, multiple rocket launchers, tanks, surface-to-air systems, infantry fighting vehicles. The sheet publishes a “delivery rate” by category and by country, measured against the COMMITTED (“Committed / Delivered” columns), not against the allocated — a distinction that forbids mapping those rates back onto the allocated amounts. Nothing there covers ammunition, drones, spare parts or maintenance.

kiel-ust-r30-maindata.title: Ukraine Support Tracker — Release 30, sheet “Bilateral Assistance, MAIN DATA” (line-by-line database, 5,820 activities, column “tot_value_deliv_EUR”)
kiel-ust-r30-maindata.organisation: Kiel Institute for the World Economy
kiel-ust-r30-maindata.note: The raw database behind every figure sheet, 80 columns. It carries a “tot_value_deliv_EUR” column — the euro value of what has been delivered — and counting it is what measures the exact size of the gap: the field is almost always empty. The fill count reported below is a count performed here on this database, not a figure published by the publisher, and it is flagged as such.

reserves-ru|1er octobre 2021|cbr-reserve.confidenceWhy: A figure published by the issuer itself, read off a timestamped archive. No conversion, no interpolation.
reserves-ru|1er octobre 2021|cbr-reserve.why: This is the exact date on which the game's first turn opens — autumn 2021 — and the engine therefore carries this value, to the unit. The quarter is a quarter of peace: nothing is frozen, the reserves are available in full.

reserves-ru|12 février 2024 — total immo.date: 12 February 2024 — total immobilised by the G7, the EU and Australia
reserves-ru|12 février 2024 — total immo.confidenceWhy: The perimeter is exactly the one sought and the amount is written out in words by the Council, but it is a rounded order of magnitude fixed in February 2024, never refreshed since, and denominated in euros rather than dollars.
reserves-ru|12 février 2024 — total immo.why: This is the gap in the database being filled: the €210bn already present covered the European Union alone, whereas the actual freeze extends to the G7 and Australia for some €260bn, more than two thirds of it in the Union. What this figure does NOT say: the breakdown by jurisdiction, the Australian share, and how things have moved since February 2024. Nor does it say how many of those assets are matured securities that have become cash — the European Parliament suggests as much as 90%, which changes the nature of the immobilised asset without changing its amount. Finally, the date matters: the Council publishes this total two years AFTER the freeze, so that no official source quantifies the immobilisation on the day of 28 February 2022 itself.

reserves-ru|18 février 2022|cbr-reserves.confidenceWhy: Same series. It is the last point published before the invasion of 24 February, and the central bank stopped publishing thereafter.
reserves-ru|18 février 2022|cbr-reserves.why: Not retained, but it is the historical peak of the fund, and it falls six days before the invasion. It sets an upper bound on everything Russia could have had in hand on the first day of the war.

reserves-ru|Hiver 2022 — valeur du moteu.confidenceWhy: The size of the freeze is no longer arbitrary: it falls BETWEEN the two published totals. The EU Council quantifies €260bn immobilised by the G7, the EU and Australia in February 2024, about $281bn at the exchange rate of the time; the EPRS puts forward €289.5bn in 2025, about $318bn. The engine removes 301.9. What remains uncertain is the exchange rate used and the reporting date, not the order of magnitude.
reserves-ru|Hiver 2022 — valeur du moteu.why: The freeze is played on the turn of the invasion and removes $301.9bn from the $611.9bn of the opening position, which leaves 310. Be careful what that number represents: it is what Russia can SPEND, and no source publishes it. The Bank of Russia never splits its reserves between a frozen share and an available one — its own figures go on counting the immobilised assets, which is why the published series does not fall: $643bn in February 2022, 598 at the end of 2023, 754 at the end of 2025. The engine therefore does not model the total Moscow displays, it models the till actually open, obtained by subtraction. It is a derived quantity, and it must be read as such.

reserves-ru|Année 2025 — total immobilis.date: Year 2025 — total immobilised across all jurisdictions, Switzerland included
reserves-ru|Année 2025 — total immobilis.confidenceWhy: A compilation by the EPRS drawn from calculations by PISM and the Swiss federal government, not from an official declaration by the holding jurisdictions; the EPRS itself writes that the exact value per jurisdiction is hard to establish for want of consistent official information, and it deliberately uses a cautious figure for Luxembourg.
reserves-ru|Année 2025 — total immobilis.why: Retained solely to BRACKET the Council's figure, never to replace it: the perimeter differs, since it adds Switzerland — €6.2bn — and does not isolate Australia. Its real value lies elsewhere, in the concentration it reveals: out of €289.5bn, 209.2 sit in the Union and 180 in Belgium alone, that is 62% of the world total with a single custodian. The Western freeze therefore rests on a Belgian decision, which no aggregate amount would let you guess.

reserves-ru|28 février 2022|conseil-ue-s.confidenceWhy: The amount is published by the Council, but it covers the European Union ONLY and it is denominated in euros. The total immobilised by all the partners together is higher and is not quantified on that page.
reserves-ru|28 février 2022|conseil-ue-s.why: This is the only immobilisation we have been able to verify at source. It dates the freeze — third sanctions package, February 2022 — but it is not enough to quantify what Russia actually lost.

reserves-ru|30 juin 2026|cbr-reserves-ar.confidenceWhy: Read off a snapshot timestamped 23 July 2026, on a page its publisher dates 1 July 2026.
reserves-ru|30 juin 2026|cbr-reserves-ar.why: To be set, on the same day, against the $46.4bn of the sovereign fund that can actually be mobilised. A ratio of fifteen to one between what Russia declares it holds and what its Treasury can commit: that is the gap the database has to preserve, failing which reading the reserves alone would give Russia a financial power far above the reality.

reserves-ru|30 juin 2026 — dont or monét.confidenceWhy: The “gold” column of the central bank's table, read off a timestamped snapshot; no conversion.
reserves-ru|30 juin 2026 — dont or monét.why: Gold accounts for 41.5% of the $720.4bn declared at that date. It is the only item in the reserves that has genuinely grown since 2021, and it is also the only one that can be said to be physically beyond the reach of sanctions. It does not follow that it is spendable: shifting $300bn of gold on markets closed to Russian counterparties is a separate question, on which the source is silent.

reserves-ru|31 décembre 2021|cbr-reserve.why: Not retained: the engine does not replay the pre-war trajectory, it opens on it. This point serves as a control — it shows that the fund is still RISING while the army masses, which the game does not represent.

reserves-ru|31 mars 2022|cbr-reserves-me.confidenceWhy: A value published by the central bank itself, but read on the live page: no timestamped snapshot available covers that month, and today's display therefore does not prove the display of the time.
reserves-ru|31 mars 2022|cbr-reserves-me.why: The most important point of this whole item, and it comes down to a subtraction. Five weeks after the freeze, declared reserves fall only from $617.1bn at the end of February to $606.4bn at the end of March, a drop of $10.7bn — when some $300bn had just been immobilised. The conclusion is mechanical: the Bank of Russia GOES ON counting the frozen assets in its published total. Every part of the series after February 2022 therefore measures what Russia owns on paper, never what it can mobilise, and the central bank publishes no breakdown between the two.

reserves-ru|31 décembre 2023|cbr-reserve.confidenceWhy: Read off a snapshot timestamped 2 July 2024, on a page its publisher dates 1 June 2024.
reserves-ru|31 décembre 2023|cbr-reserve.why: Two years after the freeze, the displayed total is almost back to its end-2021 level. That does not mean Russia has recovered its assets: the frozen share is still counted in it, and the recovery comes from gold, whose value rises from $133.1bn at the end of 2021 to $155.9bn at this date.

reserves-ru|31 décembre 2024|cbr-reserve.confidenceWhy: Read off a snapshot timestamped 23 March 2025, on a page its publisher dates 1 March 2025.
reserves-ru|31 décembre 2024|cbr-reserve.why: Three years after the freeze, the total is stable. Beneath that stability, a complete switch of composition: foreign exchange reserves proper fall to $413.4bn while gold rises to $195.7bn, that is 32% of the total against 21% at the end of 2021.

reserves-ru|31 décembre 2025|cbr-reserve.confidenceWhy: Read off a snapshot timestamped 23 July 2026, on a page its publisher dates 1 July 2026.
reserves-ru|31 décembre 2025|cbr-reserve.why: The total exceeds its pre-war peak of $643.2bn for the first time. The explanation lies in a single line: gold is worth $326.5bn, against $133.1bn at the end of 2021. Foreign exchange reserves, for their part, stand at $428.3bn and have not moved in two years. A rise in valuation, then, not a replenishment — and it bears largely on assets that remain immobilised.

reserves-ru|31 juillet 2026|cbr-reserves.confidenceWhy: The last point published as at the capture date, and therefore later than the last timestamped snapshot available: it can only be read on the live page.
reserves-ru|31 juillet 2026|cbr-reserves.why: The most recent point in the series. It confirms the plateau reached: the total no longer advances, gold ebbs slightly to $292.9bn and foreign exchange reserves stay inert at $427.5bn.
